'''Alan Coffman Cummings''' (born in 1944) is an American astrophysicist and cosmic ray researcher who has served as a Senior Research Scientist at the [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech) since 1973.<ref name="caltech50">{{cite web |title=Voyager Scientist Celebrates 50 Years at Caltech |date=June 23, 2023 |url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/voyager-scientist-celebrates-50-years-at-caltech |publisher=California Institute of Technology }}</ref> He is best known as an investigator of NASA's [[Voyager program]]'s [[Cosmic Ray Subsystem]] and as a leading expert on galactic cosmic rays in interstellar space.<ref name="nasa">{{cite web |title=Alan Cummings |url=https://science.nasa.gov/people/alan-cummings/ |publisher=NASA Science}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Alan Coffman Cummings grew up in [[Wichita Falls, Texas]]. He was the youngest child, with two brothers and a sister. He had a competitive family where academic excellence was standard, his older brother was a state football champion and his sister a junior tennis champion. Cummings also played tennis.<ref name="heritage">{{cite web |title=Alan Cummings, Astrophysicist, Cosmic Ray Researcher, and Voyager Mission Scientist |date=July 3, 2023 |url=https://heritageproject.caltech.edu/interviews-updates/alan-cummings |publisher=Caltech Heritage Project }}</ref> His father worked in a [[peanut]] distribution business after the [[Great Depression]] forced him out of teaching mathematics.<ref name="heritage"/>

Cummings attended [[Rice University]] when it had a free tuition period. Before that, he received a tennis scholarship from the [[University of Oklahoma]], but his mother "shot that down" as it was not enough to cover the full tuition. After Rice, he spent a year at [[Cambridge University]] in England on a [[Winston Churchill Memorial Trusts|Winston Churchill Foundation Fellowship]], where he first considered becoming an astronaut after corresponding with [[Alan Shepard]] by mail. Cummings spent two summers working at [[Los Alamos Laboratory]] on [[Project Vela]], which detected nuclear tests.<ref name="heritage"/>

{{Quote box
| quote = ... I took a course in space physics, and when I got to the cosmic ray part of that course, I said, "This is the most boring thing I can imagine. I'm not going into this." And of course it's exactly what I went into and what I've been doing ever since.
| source = Alan Cummings<ref name="heritage"/>
| width = 30%
| align = right
}}

Cummings arrived at [[Caltech]] as a graduate student in 1967, joining the Space Radiation Laboratory under [[Rochus Eugen Vogt]] and [[Edward C. Stone]].<ref name="caltech50"/><ref name="heritage"/> He earned his PhD in physics in 1973 with a thesis on [[cosmic ray]] positrons and electrons based on balloon-borne experiments launched from [[Fort Churchill, Manitoba]], Canada.<ref name="caltech50"/>

[[File:Voyager's Cosmic Ray Subsystem.png|thumb|Cosmic Ray Subsystem]]
According to Cummings, his career took a decisive turn in mid-1973 when his PhD thesis experiment, a cosmic ray detector carried by balloon to the edge of the atmosphere, malfunctioned and drifted over the Soviet Union.<ref name="caltech50"/><ref name="heritage"/> He was able to retrieve the wreckage after a trip to Moscow, but the equipment was too damaged to rebuild. Cummings described the failure to be "fortunate in a way"<ref name="caltech50"/> because after it he was hired as a staff scientist to work on [[Voyager program|Voyager]]'s [[Cosmic Ray Subsystem]] (CRS), led by Vogt and Stone, skipping a [[postdoc]] position.<ref name="caltech50"/> He took part in development and testing of the low-energy telescopes and electron telescope components.<ref name="nasa"/><ref name="heritage"/>

Cummings is the last person who physically touched both Voyager spacecraft before launch in 1977, performing final inspections of the telescope windows a few days before launch.<ref name="nasa"/><ref name="caltech50"/> Cummings has worked at Caltech and on the Voyager mission for more than 50 years.<ref name="caltech50"/> He became CRS's principal investigator after Ed Stone's retirement.

As part of the CRS team, Cummings was involved in measuring the composition and energy spectra of galactic cosmic rays in interstellar space, what he calls "the holy grail of cosmic ray physics".<ref name="heritage"/> When [[Voyager 1]] crossed into [[interstellar space]] in 2012, it provided first direct measurements of cosmic rays beyond the solar system's influence.<ref name="nasa"/><ref name="heritage"/>

Beyond Voyager, Cummings worked on cosmic ray detectors for other spacecraft missions, including [[ISEE-3]], ACE ([[Advanced Composition Explorer]]), [[STEREO]] (twin solar observatories), and [[Parker Solar Probe]]'s [[EPI-Hi]] instrument.<ref name="heritage"/>  He has delivered three Theodore von Kármán Lectures at JPL (2007, 2012, and 2017).<ref name="caltech50"/>

== Caltech Bird Walks ==
In 1986, Cummings co-founded Caltech's weekly [[birdwatching]] group with Ernie Franzgrote. At that time, he had already been birdwatching for nearly 20 years; all of his siblings are also birdwatchers.<ref name="heritage"/> {{As of|2023}}, the group has conducted over 1,700 walks, with Cummings meticulously documenting every sighting.<ref name="caltech50"/> He maintains detailed data of bird populations on campus, noting long-term trends and seasonal patterns.<ref name="caltech50"/> A newspaper article from 1998 claimed that Cummings "spotted 450 out of a total 750 [[List of birds of the United States|U.S. species]]".<ref>{{cite web |title=Caltech Birding - Publicity |url=http://birdwalks.caltech.edu/publicity.html |website=birdwalks.caltech.edu |access-date=June 25, 2025 |archive-date=April 12, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250412003249/http://birdwalks.caltech.edu/publicity.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Cummings met his wife Suzette on her birthday in March 1973 while he was at Caltech delivering his thesis for printing.<ref name="caltech50"/><ref name="heritage"/> They had their first date six days later, on his birthday, and married in October 1973.<ref name="caltech50"/><ref name="heritage"/> Their son was born in 1975.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://heritageproject.caltech.edu/interviews/suzette-cummings|title=Suzette Cummings|website=Heritage Project}}</ref> Suzette worked in various administrative roles at Caltech for over 40 years. She was recognized as an honorary alumna in 2001.<ref name="caltech50"/>

== Selected publications ==
According to his Bibliography page<ref>{{cite web |url=https://sites.srl.caltech.edu/~ace/bibliography_acc.html |title=Bibliography |publisher=Caltech}}</ref> Cummings has authored or coauthored 172 papers in peer-reviewed journals. According to his Google Scholar page, 57 of those have been cited more than 13,000 times as of 2025.
